children: Tata Sons’ board has resolved to begin steps to comply with the Reserve Bank of India’s regulatory framework, days after the central bank rejected the holding company’s application to surrender its registration as a core investment company (CIC).

“The Board also resolved to initiate steps to comply with the applicable RBI guidelines and will seek guidance from RBI, Tata Trusts and other stakeholders on applicable compliance requirements,” Tata Sons said in a statement following its September 17 board meeting.
The resolution marks a shift towards regulatory compliance after Tata Sons spent more than two years seeking to exit the RBI framework, which is likely to pave the way for a listing of Tata Sons.

The RBI introduced its scale-based regulatory framework for non-banking financial companies in October 2021. Under the framework, an NBFC classified in the Upper Layer must list its shares within three years of identification. Tata Sons was first designated an NBFC-Upper Layer in September 2022, setting a listing deadline of September 30, 2025.

Tata Sons sought to avoid the listing requirement by repaying over Rs 21,000 crore of debt during FY24 and applying in March 2024 to surrender its CIC registration. The company argued that after becoming debt-free and ceasing to borrow, it no longer needed to remain registered as an NBFC.
The RBI, however, rejected the application through a letter dated September 11, 2026, bringing the listing requirement back into focus.
According to media reports, the central bank has also filed a caveat before the Bombay High Court, ensuring that it is heard before any interim order is passed if Tata Sons challenges the rejection.
The latest board resolution also brings Tata Sons’ regulatory obligations into conflict with the position previously taken by its controlling shareholder.
Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has opposed converting Tata Sons into a listed company and has favoured exploring alternatives that would preserve its privately held structure.

In July 2025, Tata Trusts passed a resolution directing the Tata Sons board to do everything possible to keep the holding company private, while exploring ways to provide an exit to the Shapoorji Pallonji Group. Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran was asked to examine all available options to meet these objectives.
Consultations with Tata Trusts will therefore be critical. The charitable trusts - referred to as Tata Trusts - collectively own about 66 percent of Tata Sons.
The Shapoorji Pallonji Group, which holds around 18.4 percent, the company’s largest minority shareholder has supported a listing as a potential route to monetise its stake.

title: Tata Sons board says it will initiate steps to comply with RBI listing norms
